body:
Understanding the early-medieval period

The period from approximately the 7th to the 12th century CE witnessed important changes in India's political organisation, agriculture and society. Large kingdoms continued to exist, but many regional dynasties also became powerful. Local chiefs, landholding families and military commanders increasingly influenced the government of their territories.

The death of Harshavardhana in the 7th century weakened the political unity that he had established over parts of northern India. However, this did not mean that the entire subcontinent became politically disorganised. Different regions developed their own kingdoms, administrative arrangements and centres of economic and cultural activity.

Three connected developments help explain this transition: the growing power of regional chiefs, the expansion of agriculture and the emergence of ruling dynasties from different social backgrounds.

Samantas and the formation of new states

A samanta was a subordinate ruler, chief or powerful landholder who acknowledged the authority of a stronger king. The relationship commonly involved military service, attendance at the royal court and the presentation of gifts or tribute.

By the 7th century, several kings depended on powerful chiefs to help administer territory and provide soldiers. The overlord benefited from their support, while the chiefs enjoyed local authority and access to resources.

When a samanta accumulated sufficient wealth, military strength and political support, the relationship could change. He might adopt titles such as maha-samanta or maha-mandaleshvara, meaning a powerful subordinate chief or lord of a large region. Some eventually challenged their overlords and established independent kingdoms.

Thus, the same network that helped an established king govern a large territory could also produce rival rulers when central authority weakened.

The rise of the Rashtrakutas

The Rashtrakutas provide a clear example. They were initially subordinate to the Chalukyas of Karnataka. In the middle of the 8th century, Dantidurga, a Rashtrakuta chief, overthrew his Chalukya overlord and established an independent political position in the Deccan.

Dantidurga also performed a ritual called hiranyagarbha, literally the golden womb. The ritual was associated with the claim that the person performing it was symbolically reborn as a Kshatriya. It helped a successful ruler present his newly acquired political position as socially legitimate.

The ritual illustrates an important distinction: military success could establish actual control, while religious ceremonies and royal titles could strengthen claims to legitimacy.

Political power was not based on birth alone

Some ruling families emerged from backgrounds not traditionally associated with kingship. The NCERT account mentions Mayurasharman of the Kadambas and Harichandra of the Gurjara-Pratiharas as Brahmanas who took up arms and established kingdoms in Karnataka and Rajasthan respectively.

This shows that military organisation, control of resources and recognition by other influential groups were important in the formation of early-medieval states. A ruler's declared social status and his actual political power were related but were not identical.

Administration and resources

Early-medieval kings obtained resources from peasants, cattle-keepers, craftspeople and traders. Revenue maintained the court, officials and armed forces. It also supported the construction of temples and forts.

Royal administration was not equally direct everywhere. Kings often shared practical authority with samantas, local landholders, village organisations and influential religious institutions. Administrative and military positions could become hereditary, passing from one generation of a family to the next.

Consequently, a king who claimed a grand title such as maharajadhiraja, or great king above other kings, did not necessarily exercise direct control over every village within his claimed territory.

Prelims focus

  • The early-medieval transition is commonly studied from approximately the 7th to the 12th century CE.
  • A samanta was a subordinate chief expected to support an overlord, including through military service.
  • Dantidurga established Rashtrakuta independence from the Chalukyas in the middle of the 8th century.
  • Hiranyagarbha was a ritual associated with a claim to Kshatriya status.
  • Mayurasharman is associated with the Kadambas; Harichandra is associated with the Gurjara-Pratiharas.
  • Trap: A ruler's impressive title did not automatically mean that all local chiefs had lost their authority.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Tracing Changes Through a Thousand Years', printed pp. 6–11; ch. 2, 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed pp. 16–19; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, 'New Empires and Kingdoms', printed pp. 116–117.]

title: The Early-Medieval Transition: How Regional Kingdoms Emerged

body:
What was a land grant?

Land was a major source of wealth in early-medieval India because agriculture supported a large part of the population and provided revenue to rulers. Kings and other powerful donors made grants of land or rights connected with land to Brahmanas, temples, religious institutions and other beneficiaries.

A land grant was a formal transfer of land or specified rights over land to a recipient. Depending on the terms of the grant, these rights could include receiving agricultural revenue, collecting particular taxes or enjoying specified exemptions.

A land grant should not always be understood as a modern sale of private property. The precise rights transferred depended on the grant. In some cases, cultivators continued working the same fields while the person or institution entitled to receive particular payments changed.

Why rulers made land grants

Land grants served several purposes. Rulers could reward religious specialists, support temples and educational institutions, secure the cooperation of influential families or maintain officials and military supporters. In suitable regions, grants could also encourage the extension of cultivation to previously uncultivated land.

These purposes were connected. A grant to a religious institution could strengthen the ruler's prestige while supplying the institution with regular income. A grant to a military supporter could help sustain soldiers without requiring the king to pay every expense directly from the royal treasury.

Copper plates and the rights recorded in grants

Many grants were recorded on copper-plate inscriptions. Such records could identify the donor and recipient, describe the land and its boundaries, and specify the rights granted. Some plates were joined by a ring bearing a royal seal.

An important distinction is that a copper-plate grant normally recorded an administrative or legal act, while a prashasti was a text praising a ruler. A prashasti might celebrate victories and royal qualities in exaggerated language. A land-grant record might also contain praise, but its clauses concerning land, boundaries and revenue served a different purpose.

Important categories of land

Chola inscriptions provide several useful terms for distinguishing landholders and beneficiaries. These terms refer to different categories and should not all be treated as identical kinds of donation.

TermMeaningExam distinction
BrahmadeyaLand granted to BrahmanasAssociated with Brahmana settlements and their assemblies
DevadanaLand donated to a templeSupports a religious institution
ShalabhogaLand assigned for the maintenance of a schoolEducational purpose
PallichchhandamLand donated to Jaina institutionsJaina institutional beneficiary
VellanvagaiLand of non-Brahmana peasant proprietorsA landholding category, not a synonym for a royal grant

Another term, agrahara, is commonly used for a settlement or grant associated with Brahmanas. The terms used in inscriptions varied by region and period. Therefore, the category and the beneficiary should be identified from the actual context rather than assumed to be identical throughout India.

The effect on villages

Consider a village where cultivators produce grain and owe a portion of the harvest as revenue. If a ruler grants the right to receive that revenue to a temple, the cultivators may continue farming while the temple becomes entitled to the specified payment. Some grants also allowed beneficiaries to collect other dues or exercise limited administrative rights.

Thus, the important question is not simply who received land, but which rights over its produce, revenue and administration were transferred. The answer could differ from one grant to another.

Land grants could support agrarian expansion, but not every grant involved clearing a forest or founding a new village. Grants could also concern land that was already under cultivation.

Prelims focus

  • Brahmadeya refers to land granted to Brahmanas.
  • Devadana refers to land given to temples.
  • Shalabhoga is associated with the maintenance of a school.
  • Pallichchhandam is associated with Jaina institutions.
  • Copper plates were used to record grants and could bear a royal seal.
  • Trap: Vellanvagai denotes land of non-Brahmana peasant proprietors; it is not another name for brahmadeya.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 2, 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed pp. 18–20 and 26–27; IGNOU, BHIC-105, Unit 10, section 10.3, 'Agrarian Economy' (online, consulted 19 November 2026); IGNOU, BHIC-132, Unit 13, 'Land, Revenue Systems and Agrarian Relations, c. 700–1200 CE' (online, consulted 19 November 2026).]

title: Land Grants: Revenue Rights, Beneficiaries and Rural Administration

body:
How cultivation expanded

During the early-medieval centuries, cultivation spread into new areas in several regions of India. Forests were cleared in some places, land was levelled and settlements grew around fields, water sources and religious establishments. The speed and extent of these changes differed from region to region.

The growth of agriculture increased the amount of produce available to cultivators, local landholders and rulers. More cultivated land could provide more revenue, helping rulers maintain armies, officials, forts and temples. Agrarian expansion and the growth of regional states therefore reinforced one another.

The process also affected communities living in forests and pastoral areas. Some moved elsewhere, while others adopted cultivation or combined it with existing occupations. As villages became part of wider political and economic networks, their inhabitants increasingly encountered revenue collectors, chiefs, traders and religious institutions.

Irrigation and the Kaveri delta

The Kaveri delta in present-day Tamil Nadu illustrates how better control of water could support agricultural expansion. Branches of the river deposited fertile soil and provided moisture, particularly suited to rice cultivation. However, natural fertility alone was insufficient for dependable farming in every field.

Settlers and rulers undertook practical works such as clearing vegetation, levelling land, constructing embankments, digging canals and maintaining irrigation tanks. Wells also supplied water in suitable locations.

An embankment could help control floodwater, while a canal could direct water from a river or tank to a field. A tank stored water that could be released when required. Such works needed labour, planning and continuing maintenance; building them once was not enough.

More reliable irrigation allowed larger areas to be cultivated and sometimes supported more than one crop in a year. Increased production could sustain larger populations and provide a stronger economic base for local institutions and states.

The social consequences of expansion

Agrarian growth did not make every peasant equally prosperous. Some households controlled fertile land or cattle, while others depended heavily on labour and less productive plots. Certain groups also combined farming with crafts during periods when agricultural work was limited.

As occupations and local power relationships became more varied, communities were organised into different jatis, or social groups. Their relative position could vary between regions. Local assemblies of elders sometimes regulated community affairs, but villages also remained subject to the authority of landholders, chiefs and rulers.

Village institutions under the Cholas

The Chola kingdom offers clear examples of institutions connected with expanding cultivation.

InstitutionAssociated group or areaMain distinction
UrVillage settlement or assembly in non-Brahmana peasant areasLocal village affairs
SabhaAssembly of prominent Brahmana landholders in a brahmadeya settlementManagement of granted lands and local matters
NaduGroup of villagesFunctions above the individual village level
NagaramAssociation of merchantsCommercial and sometimes administrative functions

These were not identical institutions. A sabha was associated with Brahmana landholding settlements, whereas a nagaram was connected with merchants. A nadu was a territorial grouping of villages rather than simply another name for a single village assembly.

The Chola inscriptions from Uttaramerur describe committees dealing with matters such as gardens, irrigation and temples. They also prescribe qualifications for committee membership. These arrangements should not be confused with universal adult-franchise elections: participation depended on conditions such as landholding, age and knowledge.

Taxes, temples and economic activity

Chola inscriptions mention kadamai as land revenue and vetti as labour demanded rather than a cash payment. Taxes and other obligations helped maintain political institutions, although the burden on producers could vary.

Temples were often important economic centres as well as places of worship. Land donated to a temple could supply food and income for priests, cooks, musicians, craft workers and others employed there. Settlements and markets could grow near major temple complexes.

The relationship was therefore broader than religion alone: agriculture supplied institutional income, institutions supported specialised occupations, and these activities contributed to the development of local settlements.

Prelims focus

  • The Kaveri delta supported agricultural expansion through fertile deposits and irrigation works.
  • The Chola ur was associated with village communities; the sabha with Brahmana landholding settlements.
  • A nadu was a grouping of villages; a nagaram was associated with merchants.
  • Uttaramerur inscriptions describe the organisation of sabha committees.
  • In Chola inscriptions, kadamai refers to land revenue and vetti to compulsory labour.
  • Trap: A sabha and a nagaram were not interchangeable names for the same organisation.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, ch. 1, 'Tracing Changes Through a Thousand Years', printed pp. 7–9; ch. 2, 'New Kings and Kingdoms', printed pp. 18 and 23–28; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, 'New Empires and Kingdoms', printed pp. 116–117; IGNOU, BHIC-105, Unit 10, section 10.3, 'Agrarian Economy' (online, consulted 19 November 2026).]
